pageTitle: Baritone Guitars: Go Lower, Go Deeper
subtitle: Explore the deep, powerful world of extended-range guitars

introduction.title: Baritone Guitars: Go Lower, Go Deeper
introduction.text: A baritone guitar reaches its lower range by physically lengthening the neck rather than by loosening standard strings, which is the detail that makes it work at all. Drop a regular guitar's low E down to B and the string goes slack and floppy; put that same B on a longer scale length and the added distance restores enough tension to keep the string taut and in tune. That's the whole appeal of the format — deep, guitar-shaped tones without the wobbly pitch and dead sustain that comes from simply detuning a standard-scale instrument too far.

columns.title: Baritone Advantages
columns.text: Because the scale length does the work instead of slack strings, a baritone gets genuinely low pitches while still holding pitch cleanly and ringing with full sustain, something a standard guitar tuned down a fourth or fifth can't manage. That combination of range and stability is why the instrument shows up equally in down-tuned metal, atmospheric film scoring, and country records that need a deep, resonant low end without switching to an actual bass.

cards.title: Scale Length
cards.description: The defining characteristic of baritone guitars is their extended scale length, typically 27-30 inches compared to standard guitars' 24.75-25.5 inches. That extra length is what lets a baritone carry lower-tuned strings without them going slack: string tension depends on scale length as well as pitch, so stretching the distance between nut and bridge restores the tautness a standard-scale string would lose if tuned down to the same note.

cards.title: Tuning Range
cards.description: Baritones are typically tuned a fourth or fifth lower than standard guitars, providing access to much deeper frequencies while maintaining playability. Landing a fourth or fifth down rather than further is a deliberate compromise: go lower still and even the extended scale starts to run out of usable tension, while staying within that range keeps familiar chord shapes and standard technique largely intact.

fields.label: Standard Tuning
fields.value: E-A-D-G-B-E

fields.label: Baritone Standard
fields.value: B-E-A-D-F#-B

fields.label: Low Range
fields.value: Down to A or even lower

cards.title: Scale Length Options
cards.description: There's no single 'correct' baritone scale length because the right choice depends on how far down you're tuning: a 27-inch scale feels closer to a standard guitar and suits the more modest B-standard tuning, while a full 30-inch scale is built for tunings that go a fifth or more below standard without the strings turning to rubber. Multi-scale or fanned-fret designs push this further by giving each string its own effective scale length, so the low strings get maximum tension while the high strings stay comfortable to bend.
items: 27" Scale: Shorter baritone scale, closer to standard guitar feel
28-28.5" Scale: Most common baritone scale length, balanced tension
30" Scale: Extended scale for maximum low-end clarity
Multi-Scale/Fanned: Different scale lengths per string for optimal tension

cards.title: Construction Differences
cards.description: Heavier strings and a longer neck both add real physical load, which is why baritones typically ship with reinforced necks and internal bracing rather than reusing a standard guitar's specifications at a longer scale. The larger bodies common on baritones aren't just for looks either — a bigger cavity moves more air and reinforces the lower frequencies the instrument is built to produce, the same way a dreadnought outperforms a parlor guitar on bass response.
items: Reinforced Neck: Stronger construction to handle increased string tension
Larger Body: Often bigger than standard guitars for better low-end resonance
Heavy-Gauge Strings: Typically .013-.072 or heavier for proper tension
Adjusted Bracing: Internal bracing optimized for lower frequencies

cards.title: Acoustic Baritone
cards.description: An acoustic baritone channels its lower tuning straight into a bigger top and body rather than an amp, which produces a woody, naturally compressed low end well suited to solo fingerpicking and songwriting. Because there's no pickup shaping the tone, the instrument's low-end character comes entirely from its size and bracing, which is why acoustic baritones tend to run larger than standard-body acoustics.

fields.label: Characteristics
fields.value: Rich, woody low-end resonance; perfect for fingerpicking and folk; natural compression and sustain; ideal for songwriting and recording

fields.label: Best for
fields.value: Country, folk, Americana, cinematic music, solo performance

fields.label: Notable models
fields.value: Martin Grand J-28LSE Baritone, Taylor Custom Baritone, Santa Cruz Baritone

cards.title: Electric Baritone
cards.description: An electric baritone pushes its low end through pickups and an amp, which is what lets it stay articulate even under heavy distortion — a gain stage that would turn a down-tuned standard guitar into mud instead tightens up because the extended scale keeps the strings taut. That clarity under distortion is exactly why the format took off in metal and progressive rock, genres that need low pitches without losing note definition.

fields.label: Characteristics
fields.value: Aggressive attack and definition; perfect for heavy, distorted tones; extended range for lead work; effects processing possibilities

fields.label: Best for
fields.value: Metal, progressive rock, experimental music, film scoring

fields.label: Notable models
fields.value: Fender Bass VI, PRS SE 277, Schecter Hellraiser

cards.title: Metal & Heavy Rock
cards.description: Baritones excel in heavy music genres where low tunings are essential, since the extended scale keeps palm-muted riffs tight and articulate at pitches that would turn to mush on a standard-scale guitar tuned down to match.

fields.label: Key Techniques
fields.value: Down-tuned riffing, extended range solos, heavy rhythm work, djent and progressive styles

fields.label: Notable Artists
fields.value: Meshuggah, Periphery, Animals as Leaders, TesseracT

cards.title: Alternative & Indie
cards.description: Unique tonal character adds depth to alternative and experimental music, where the baritone's darker, more resonant voice works as a texture and atmosphere instrument rather than a lead one.

fields.label: Key Techniques
fields.value: Atmospheric textures, chord voicings, melodic bass lines, ambient soundscapes

fields.label: Notable Artists
fields.value: Cure, My Bloody Valentine, Sonic Youth, Godspeed You! Black Emperor

cards.title: Country & Americana
cards.description: Baritones provide rich, deep accompaniment in country and folk contexts, continuing a tradition that dates back to Duane Eddy's late-1950s recordings, which first brought the instrument's deep, twangy voice into popular music.

fields.label: Key Techniques
fields.value: Fingerpicking patterns, open chord voicings, slide guitar, rhythmic strumming

fields.label: Notable Artists
fields.value: Duane Eddy, Pat Green, Cross Canadian Ragweed, Jason Isbell

cards.title: Film & Game Scoring
cards.description: Perfect for creating atmospheric and cinematic soundscapes, since a baritone's low, resonant sustain fills the same low-mid space an orchestra would otherwise need strings or brass to cover.

fields.label: Key Techniques
fields.value: Ambient textures, drone notes, harmonic intervals, effects processing

fields.label: Notable Artists
fields.value: Hans Zimmer, Trent Reznor, Gustavo Santaolalla, Austin Wintory

cards.title: A Unique Instrument
cards.description: The Fender Bass VI, introduced in 1961, is perhaps the most famous baritone guitar. With its 30-inch scale and unique tuning (an octave below standard guitar), it occupies a special place between guitar and bass — closer to a six-string baritone than a true bass, which is why guitarists rather than bassists have historically been the ones drawn to it.

fields.label: Specifications
fields.value: 30" scale length; E-A-D-G-B-E tuning (octave below guitar); three single-coil pickups; Jaguar-style body and electronics; floating bridge with vibrato

fields.label: Famous Users
fields.value: The Beatles (John Lennon played it on 'Back in the U.S.S.R.' and 'The Long and Winding Road'), The Cure (Robert Smith has used one as his primary tone on many tracks since Faith), Cream (Jack Bruce)

cards.title: Rhythm Techniques
cards.description: A baritone's low tuning and long scale mean power chords and palm-muted riffs come out thicker and more defined than the same shapes played on a detuned standard guitar, since the extra string tension keeps the notes from turning into an indistinct rumble under gain.
items: Power chords: Massive, thick sound in low register
Open chords: Rich, complex voicings
Palm muting: Percussive attack for metal styles
Drone notes: Sustained low notes under melodies
Chord extensions: Use the extended range for unique voicings

cards.title: Lead Techniques
cards.description: Soloing on a baritone means working in a register a standard guitar can't reach without an octave pedal, which is why baritone leads tend to sit closer to the vocal or bass range and read as darker and more atmospheric rather than as conventional shred playing.
items: Extended range solos: Access to lower melodic register
Harmonic intervals: Rich two-note harmonies
Slide guitar: Excellent for atmospheric textures
Ambient picking: Spacious, cinematic soundscapes
Cross-picking: Complex fingerpicking patterns

cards.title: Setup Considerations
cards.description: A baritone's heavier strings and longer scale change the math on setup: nut slots cut for lighter standard-gauge strings will bind or buzz once heavier gauges are installed, and intonation is more sensitive to error because small measurement mistakes get magnified over the longer distance between nut and bridge.
items: String gauge: Heavier strings needed for proper tension
Intonation: Critical due to extended scale length
Action height: May need adjustment for comfortable playing
Nut slots: Must accommodate heavier strings
Bridge adjustment: Important for tuning stability

cards.title: For Guitar Players
cards.description: Because a baritone uses the same relative tuning intervals and fretboard patterns as a standard guitar, everything you already know transfers directly — the same chord shapes and scale patterns just sound lower. What takes adjustment is physical: heavier strings under more tension require a firmer fretting hand, and the extended scale spreads frets slightly further apart, so stretches that were comfortable on a standard neck take a little recalibration.

fields.label: Familiar Territory
fields.value: Same chord shapes, different pitches; standard guitar techniques apply; familiar fretboard patterns; easy transition from 6-string guitar

fields.label: New Considerations
fields.value: Heavier string tension requires adjustment; extended scale affects finger stretches; different tonal palette to explore; may need to adjust playing style

cards.title: Practice Tips
items: Start with familiar songs: Learn songs you know in new tuning
Explore the low end: Take advantage of the extended range
Experiment with effects: Reverb and delay sound great on baritones
Play with others: Baritones complement standard guitars well
Record your playing: Hear how the baritone sits in a mix
